title: Gold and iron alike
hookLine: the one to whom praise and blame, gold and iron are the same (Salok M9, ang 1427)

lines: ONE LINE ON THE DRIVE HOME.
cards: A performance review lands in your inbox. Four paragraphs of praise, and one line that says you could communicate more clearly. Guess which line gets replayed on the drive home.
The praise fades by dinner; the criticism rides along like a stone in a shoe. Or the reverse: one big compliment and you float for days, and then you need another.
Either way, someone else's voice is holding the steering wheel. Guru Tegh Bahadur's fourteenth salok describes a person who has taken the wheel back.

teach.b: The salok begins ustat nindiaa naahi jih, kanchan loh samaan.
In paraphrase: the one for whom there is no praise and no slander, to whom gold and iron are the same: says Nanak, listen, O mind, know that one to be liberated. Ustat is praise.
Nindiaa is slander, blame, talking someone down.
Kanchan is gold, and loh is iron, the everyday metal of pots and plows.
Samaan is equal, alike. The salok doesn't say this person never gets praised or blamed. Praise and blame just have no hook to catch on.
Then it sets two metals side by side. Gold glitters; it's what we'd like to be called. Iron is ordinary.

The salok asks for the same calm when someone calls you iron as when someone calls you gold. Back on day five hundred eighty-two, in a Sorath hymn, gold and dust were seen alike. Here it's gold and iron.
The ninth Guru keeps returning to this picture, as if it's worth hearing more than once. And notice the last word: mukat, liberated.
Sikh teaching speaks of jeevan mukat, someone free while still alive.

Freedom here isn't a place you go after death. It's a person at a desk, reading a review, who can take the praise and the one line of criticism with the same steady face, learn from both, and stay themselves.
Not to stop hearing what people say, but to stop being steered by it.

how: Sikhs hear the fourteenth salok among Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks at the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and speak of jeevan mukat, being free while alive, as its ideal.

o: iron, the metal of pots and plows
praise that lifts you for days

games.q: gold and iron alike — tap the pairs.

s: the salok says the free person never gets praised or blamed
they do; praise and blame just find no hook in them.
the ninth Guru also pictures gold and dust seen alike in a Sorath hymn
the image returns, gold beside something ordinary.
in this salok, freedom is only something that comes after death
Sikhs speak of jeevan mukat, free while still alive.

games.q: your review has four paragraphs of praise and one line of criticism. what does the fourteenth salok describe?
o: hold onto the praise and ignore the rest.
take both the same, gold and iron alike.
fixate on the criticism until it's fixed.
games.why: the one with no praise and no slander, to whom gold and iron are the same, says Nanak, know that one to be free.

practice: Bring back the last compliment you got and let its little lift settle; then a recent criticism, and let its sting settle too.

Hold them side by side, like a gold coin and an iron nail in your two open hands, ask of each whether there's something true to learn, and then set both down. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths.

wordCard.voice: Kanchan, gold. The fourteenth salok says the one for whom praise and blame, kanchan and loh, iron, are the same is mukat, free.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kanchan, gold. The salok sets it beside loh, iron, and calls them the same.

carryVoice: Your line: take the wheel back. Gold or iron, the same steady face. Day five hundred ninety-four, done.

sources.ref: Salok Mahalla 9, salok 14 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427)
